#### **Europe still the focal point, but contagion not widespread...yet** 

Whilst most attention continues, justifiably, to be focused on Eurozone issues, there are signs that any contagion is not yet widespread.  Although China, and Asia in general, has emitted more mixed macroeconomic signals, the US situation has been more encouraging; US consumer confidence rose significantly in December from its August low, to 69.9, and recent

non-farm payrolls exceeded general expectation while the unemployment rate declined to a near two-year low of 8.5%.  Chinese data have indicated a slowdown, but not a particularly significant one: industrial production grew by 12.4% in November and fixed asset investment was recorded at 24.5%, both slightly lower than previously, but still indicative of a robust economy.  This was also consistent with the tighter domestic credit market during the year and the impact of weaker global demand on Chinese exports.  Nevertheless, we expect that China will have some ammunition in the face of any significant threats to growth in 2012, through reserve ratio and interest rate cuts and the ability to increase lending. 

##### **Aluminium performs “best” amongst LME metals during** 

##### **2011...** 

In terms of price, aluminium was the outperformer amongst the LME base metals in 2011, but only because its price fell the least.  The cash price closed the year at $1,995/tonne, a decline of 18.9% compared with end-2010; the copper cash price fell by 21.3% over the year whilst tin was the worst performing metal, down by 28.9%.  In fact, commodities in general underperformed, except notably crude oil, which ended the year higher.  Rebasing to 100 for January 1st 2011, the energy-heavy S&PGSCI Index ended the year at 102.1, the CRB Index at 91.7 and the DJUBS commodity Index at 86.6.  Meanwhile, base metals, as represented by the LMEX, finished at 78.5 (the Thomson Reuters GFMS Base Metals Index, which is an average of all the base metals rather than the LMEX - which is heavily weighted towards the performance of aluminium and copper - ended 2011 at 74.7 on a similarly adjusted basis). 

**...but annual average metals prices are expected to weaken in 2012 after the gains seen in 2011** In terms of average price performance amongst base metals in 2011 versus 2010, the clear winner was tin which averaged $26,021/tonne on a cash basis, an increase of 27.3%. Whilst the 2011 tin market did not prove to be quite as strong as we had envisaged at the start of 2011, it nevertheless remained tight as production remained constrained.  Despite this, prices fell over the course of the year, even while reported stocks edged lower.  An export ban by a number of Indonesian producers, initiated in October, failed to have any impact on prices and the pact fell apart as some exporters began to ship metal out of the country. We still expect a relatively tight tin market in 2012, with an annual average cash price of $24,125/tonne, 7.3% down on 2011. 

Cash copper recorded a 16.9% annual increase in its average price last year, to $8,811/tonne. On-going supplyside issues continue to underpin the copper market and will provide support going forward.  However, copper’s exposure to industrial production and its position as the metal of choice for macro-led investors have constrained upside price potential.  Although the market recovered sharply from its low in early October, prices s

eem unlikely to rechallenge last year’s peaks in the current macroeconomic environment. We continue to forecast a 100,000 tonne deficit for this year and expect prices to exceed $9,000/tonne on average in Q4. For 2012 as a whole, we are forecasting the average cash price 3.2% lower than last year, at $8,525/tonne. The lead cash price gained 11.7% in 2011, to average $2,398/tonne. Chinese demand continues to recover following the environmental clampdown on domestic battery manufacturers, whilst Chinese refined production is still struggling, as November output data (down 3.5% year-onyear) showed. Economic fears triggered and fuelled by the European sovereign debt crisis have been the main dampener on commodities and the primary cause of the growing “riskoff” mentality. This has been compounded by the “flight to safety” of assets into the US dollar (especially from the Euro) which has continued to strengthen since its recent low in May last year. As far as the physical aluminium market is concerned, continued stock builds (es

pecially recently on the LME) have signalled a weakening demand environment that has also been reflected in easing physical premiums. International Aluminium Institute (IAI) data for November showed a 50,000 tonne increase during the month in unwrought stocks of aluminium held by producers. Regionally, stock builds in North America and Asia more than offset drawdowns in Latin America and Europe. For the year through November, IAI inventories rose by 60,000 tonnes; a 119,000 tonne drawdown in Europe was offset by a similar build in North America, whilst there were increases in all other regions, except Africa. Aluminium stocks reported at major Japanese ports fell by 14,300 tonnes during November, to 208,000 tonnes, but they were virtually unchanged for the year to date (down just 2,100 tonnes). ##### **LME stocks bulge in December** Total exchange stocks of aluminium added 471,000 tonnes during 2011; this comprised a 704,000 tonne increase in LME inventories (to 4.979 million tonnes) and a 233,000 drawdown in Shanghai (to 208,000). ##### **Market outlook** Looking back at 2011 as a whole, annual average tin prices of $26,021/tonne came in 9.5% lower than our projecti

on made at the start of 2011, and bore more similarity to our low case scenario C average. In addition, two further factors can be attributed to tin’s significant underperformance during 2011.  Firstly, the disruption to the Japanese electronics industry caused by the mid-March earthquake and tsunami affected tin demand to a greater degree than the other base metals (Japanese tin usage fell 18.8% year-on-year according to our estimation). Secondly, Indonesian production significantly outperformed expectations, particularly over the first half of 2011. Accordingly, we have revised our estimated 2011 deficit to 10,000 tonnes, from a 22,000 tonne deficit projected at the start of last year. 

Going forward, our forecast remains largely unchanged from our previous report.  The tin market is still expected to fall into a deficit over the year of 2012, although this is expected to come in slightly lower at 7,000 tonnes as a result of a downgrade to our mature economy demand projections. 

The ongoing market tightness will provide upward support to prices, although the degree of any upside is expected to remain constrained over the first quarter by ongoing macroeconomic concerns and a potential release of producer stocks built up in Indonesia over previous months. Thereafter, a rebound in prices is expected over the second half of 2012, leading prices to average $25,500/tonne over the final quarter of the year.  Thomson Reuters GFMS forecast tin prices to average $24,125/tonne in 2012 as a whole. 

Downside risks to our forecasts primarily come from any further worsening of economic conditions in the Eurozone, in combination with the possibilities of slowing demand growth in the emerging markets, notably in China, which forms our **low case scenario C** .  Under this scenario, we would see prices average $17,125/tonne in 2012. 

Under our **high case scenario B** , prices are forecast to rebound earlier than expected in 2012, resulting in an annual average price of $26,500/tonne.  This will be conditional on a robust demand environment in China and stronger than expected growth in the mature economies.

Although the official zinc spot price has picked up from the recent low of $1,798/tonne, by around $120, it remains highly vulnerable to further negatively perceived news in the short-term. As such, we have revised down our quarterly price projections for 2012 (see Market outlook for more detail). The recent pick up in LME stocks also does not bode too well for prices, going forward. Inventories on the exchange have climbed by over 83,000 tonnes since reversing in early December, to around 820,000 tonnes in early January. The bulk of this material, which was built up in mid-December and ahead of the monthly prompt date of Wednesday 21st, is understood to have been due to large shorts settling outstanding positions with physical deliveries on to the exchange; primarily into Johor and New Orleans. The large inflows into the latter location, however, have had a negligible effect on physical premiums in the United States, due to the cost of importing EU-origin zinc into the country. Zinc delivered into New Orleans during December is believed to have come from Xstrata’s As

turiana plant in Spain. US contract premiums have been set at similar levels to those seen in 2011, at around $7-8/lb, on healthy order volumes. Premiums have also held firm in European contract negotiations, but some consumers have asked for “optionality” on supply volumes, fearing further demand deterioration over the second half of the year. ##### **Global demand growth remains subdued...** According to the latest data from the International Lead Zinc Study Group (ILZSG), global consumption continued to register modest growth on a year-to-date basis. **Japanese demand to pick up on latest government efforts** Japanese zinc consumption is set to benefit hugely from recent steps taken to support car manufacturers’ sales. In mid-December, the Japanese government made the decision to extend existing tax breaks on fuel efficient cars and to introduce subsidies to spark demand as part of an effort to help Japanese car makers deal with the yen’s strength. The last time these steps were instigated, auto demand increased by about 900,000 vehicles a year. The Japan Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (JAMA) believes that such stimulus measures could boost auto demand by 21% in 2012 from the 4.25 million vehicle sales the organisation expects for 2011. One key source of weakness, in terms of end-use, has been China’s auto sector, which up to November saw output increase by just 2% against the same period in 2010. This industry faced additional headwinds in the fourth quarter as a result of stricter subsidy policies on energy-saving vehicle purchases from October onwards, in addition to the newly released restrictions on car purchases for official use. ##### **...despite strong galvanised steel production** However, the galvanised steel sector, which is by far zinc’s largest end-use market, paints a different picture. According to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), galvanised plate output increased 17.6% year-on-year over the first eleven months of 2011, to 29 million tonnes. However, anecdotal sources suggest that a lack of downstream orders forced galvanising plants to operate at reduced capacities in the final two months of the year. Utilisation rates are estimated at 74% in November and 70% in December. ##### **Chinese demand continues to post modest growth...** Growth in China’s usage of zinc has also been very modest, with ILZSG suggesting demand was up just 2.3% yearon-year over the first ten months. In part, this reflects the comparatively low level of imports, which according to the latest data from the China Nonferrous Metals Industry Association (CNI-A) also increased by around 2% year-onyear over the January-November period, to 293,890 tonnes. Imports of zinc ore and concentrate were also up sharply in the month, due to relatively high treatment charges (TCs) in September and October. ##### **Market outlook** There has been no fundamental change to our 2012 market balance, except that in line with the weak economic environment we have slightly trimmed growth in global consumption. As such, Thomson Reuters GFMS is now projecting the market to be in a surplus of 218,000 tonnes, as opposed to 184,000 tonnes, previously. We have also amended our price forecast for the year, to reflect the weak economic environment. We now expect the zinc price to average $1,900/tonne over the first quarter, as opposed to $2,025/tonne, previously. We expect this to be followed by a strong recovery in line with an improving macroeconomic environment and, in turn, a pick up in zinc consumption that should see prices average $2,300/tonne over the fourth quarter, over 20% above the fourth quarter average in 2011. For 2012 as a whole, we are forecasting an annual average price of $2,115/tonne, 6% below our previous forecast of $2,250/tonne. Our high case **Scenario B** is largely based on the assumption that the debt crisis in the Eurozone is resolved faster than expected. This should see a broad-based recovery in zinc demand, which in turn should reduce the level of visible inventory. Also, with the supply pipeline fairly limited this year, we expect prices to average almost 11% above our base case forecast this year, at $2,338/tonne.
